name: United Fruit

summary.text: The United Fruit Company was a U.S. banana company and one of the largest holders of uncultivated land in Guatemala. After the government of Jacobo Árbenz enacted land reform (Decree 900) that affected the company's unused holdings, United Fruit lobbied the U.S. government for Árbenz's removal and hired public relations counsel, including Edward Bernays, to portray the government as a communist threat in the U.S. press. In August 1953 the United States authorized the CIA's Operation PBSUCCESS, which armed, funded and trained a force led by Carlos Castillo Armas that overthrew Árbenz in June 1954. The CIA's internal history of the operation and about 1,400 pages of declassified records were released in 1997.

facts.claim: Árbenz's land reform proposed redistributing unused land to be farmed by the rural majority; United Fruit was one of the largest holders of unused land in Guatemala.
facts.quote: Arbenz proposed to redistribute some of the unused land and make it available for the 90 percent to farm. Here is where the problem arose: United Fruit was one of the big holders of unused land in Guatemala.

facts.claim: On May 23, 1997 the CIA released several hundred records on the Guatemala operation, about 1,400 pages, after years of Freedom of Information Act requests; the National Security Archive published them, including an assassination instruction guide from the operation's training files.
facts.quote: These documents were among several hundred records released by the Agency on May 23, 1997.

sources.title: CIA and Assassinations: The Guatemala 1954 Documents

facts.claim: The CIA History Staff's internal account, Nicholas Cullather's 1994 report "Operation PBSUCCESS: The United States and Guatemala, 1952-1954," was later published in book form in 1999; the State Department's Foreign Relations of the United States series documented the CIA's role in a 2003 volume after it was left out of the 1983 volume.
facts.quote: The main internal history is Nicholas Cullather's 1994 CIA History Staff report, "Operation PBSUCCESS: The United States and Guatemala, 1952-1954".

facts.claim: A former United Fruit official recalled that the company spent more than $100,000 a year on Edward Bernays; Larry Tye writes that most analysts agree United Fruit was the most important force in toppling Árbenz and that Bernays was the company's most effective propagandist.
facts.quote: most analysts agree that United Fruit was the most important force in toppling Árbenz, and Bernays was the company's most effective propagandist.

sources.title: Watch Out for the Top Banana

facts.claim: Bernays arranged trips for U.S. journalists to Central America at United Fruit's expense, where they met company employees and selected figures and were presented with accounts of rising communist influence.
facts.quote: flying them to Central America on United Fruit's dime. Reporters were then introduced to company employees and handpicked societal figures while being fed a narrative of rising communist terror.

sources.title: Journey to Banana Land: How the United Fruit Company colluded with the CIA to Topple Guatemala's elected government

facts.claim: Secretary of State John Foster Dulles's former law firm, Sullivan & Cromwell, had long represented United Fruit, and CIA Director Allen Dulles had served on the company's board; John Moors Cabot of the State Department and UN Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge owned company stock, according to an educational history resource.
facts.quote: Secretary of State John Foster Dulles and his former New York law firm, Sullivan and Cromwell, had long represented the company. Allen Dulles, head of the CIA, had served on UFCO's board of trustees.

sources.publisher: University of Maryland, Baltimore County (Center for History Education)
sources.title: RS#01: Background on the Guatemalan Coup of 1954

connections.claim: United Fruit retained Edward Bernays as public relations counsel, paying more than $100,000 a year according to a former company official; he ran the company's press campaign on Guatemala in 1953–54.
connections.quote: they were spending in excess of $100,000 a year for Edward L. Bernays.

connections.claim: United Fruit lobbied for Árbenz's removal; the CIA's Operation PBSUCCESS, authorized in August 1953, overthrew his government in 1954. The CIA's internal history and declassified records describe the operation; the sources returned do not describe a contract or funding arrangement between the company and the agency.
connections.quote: Operation PBSUCCESS was authorized in August 1953. The CIA armed, funded, and trained a force of 480 men led by Carlos Castillo Armas.

openQuestions: The Dulles brothers' personal financial stakes in United Fruit differ by source (shareholders vs. stakeholders through the law firm) and rest on educational and secondary materials; Allen Dulles's board seat should be confirmed from Cullather's history or Bitter Fruit.
United Fruit's later corporate history (United Brands, Chiquita Brands International) was not sourced and is not recorded.
The CIA connection records the sequence of lobbying and the operation, not a documented relationship between the company and the agency; the owner may prefer to drop it.
